models.purpose: Represent the port logistics data-and-analytics system as a four-type network that later scoring and simulation both inherit.
models.summary: Following Carley et al. (2007) and Pestov (2009), the paper builds a meta-network whose nodes are people A1-A8, technology T1-T7, process P1-P11 and data information I1-I7, giving 33 nodes and 199 links read from government documents, institution reports and academic publications. Nine sub-networks (AT, AP, AI, TT, TP, TI, PP, PI, II) are the 0-1 relation matrices that every later formula multiplies.

variables.definition: The eight people nodes A1 to A8, from customs inspector to shipper.
The seven technology nodes T1 to T7.
The eleven process nodes P1 to P11, from vessel arrival to departure.
The seven data information nodes I1 to I7.
The 199 links among the 33 nodes.

equation_status.reason: The meta-network is defined by its node list and its 0-1 sub-network matrices in Tables 2 and 3; no governing equation is displayed.

objectives: Integrate people, technology, process and data information into one structure.
constraints: Only the four node types named in the problem statement are admitted.

parameter_estimation.method: No parameter is estimated; links are read off documents.

algorithm.convergence_criteria: Not applicable; the network is assembled by hand.

assumptions: The port business does not change significantly in the short term.
Maturity depends only on people, technology, process and data information.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The 33 nodes and 199 links are enumerated, but the link list rests on documents rather than observed operations.

validation_refs: Figure 3 draws the full meta-network and Figure 4 the nine sub-networks.
models.computational_cost: Manual assembly of 33 nodes and 199 links; no computation.
strengths: One structure serves both the scoring and the simulation.
limitations: Links come only from literature and policy documents, with no expert check.
missing_details: No criterion is given for when a document mention becomes a link.

models.purpose: Compress the twelve indicators, fed by 50 Monte Carlo deletions, into one maturity score.
models.summary: Fifty Monte Carlo runs delete elements at random from the standard network. Principal component analysis in MATLAB keeps components until 85 percent of variance is reached. The paper then reports both six components and five, and writes the maturity as a weighted sum of the twelve indicators.

objectives: Reduce twelve correlated indicators to one maturity score.
constraints: Components are kept until the cumulative variance passes 85 percent.

parameter_estimation.method: Eigenvalues of the indicator covariance from 50 Monte Carlo deletions, computed in MATLAB.

steps: Delete elements at random from the standard network, 50 times.
Compute the twelve indicators on each damaged network.
Extract principal components and keep those whose cumulative variance reaches 85 percent.
Form the maturity score as the weighted sum of the indicators.

assumptions: The illustrative enterprise represents ICM Corporation.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The demonstration uses one real firm, Mediterranean Shipping Company, but the 50 training networks are synthetic deletions.

validation_refs: Table 7 lists the first five roots and their variance shares.
The example firm scores 0.8514 against the standard network.
models.computational_cost: Fifty Monte Carlo draws plus one principal component decomposition of twelve variables.
strengths: The score is a single number a firm can be compared against.
limitations: The prose cites six components at 85 percent and then keeps five.
missing_details: Equation (8) sums its denominator only to i.
Equation (9) binds its index twice and leaves p undefined.
Equation (10) reuses the symbol of equation (7).
Equation (11) gives TAW the coefficient 0.8028 and names BIDTC and RBTC, and the twelve coefficients sum to about 1.72.

models.purpose: Simulate the average detention time of in-port transport equipment and measure the effect of three operational changes.
models.summary: A stochastic Petri net isomorphic to the meta-network is defined as a seven-tuple. Places are people, technology and data information; transitions are processes; tokens are containers or trucks. The incidence matrix gives two invariants, a thirteen-state balance gives the steady distribution, and the average delay falls from 140.167 minutes to 85.980 minutes after three changes.

objectives: Cut the average detention time of in-port transport equipment.
constraints: Places, transitions and links are inherited from the meta-network.

details: The initial marking M0 is the first component of the seven-tuple.
The steady distribution solves the global balance with the probabilities summing to one.

parameter_estimation.method: Transition delays are tabulated rather than estimated; the firing rate is the reciprocal of the delay.

steps: Map people, technology and data information to places and processes to transitions.
Build the incidence matrix and solve A X = 0 for the invariants.
Solve the global balance for the steady-state probabilities.
Divide the mean token count by the throughput to get the mean delay.
Repeat after running three transitions in parallel and replacing the manual box check.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: The thirteen state probabilities sum to one.

assumptions: There is no conflict between the needs of departments.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The delay is computed for one firm; the transition rates are assumed, not measured.

validation_refs: Table 12 gives the fourteen steady probabilities.
models.computational_cost: One linear solve of a 13-equation balance, repeated for the optimized net.
strengths: The isomorphism removes the need to design the net from scratch.
limitations: The reported 38.7 percent cut rests on assumed transition delays.
missing_details: Equation (15) sets lambda_3 x_2 equal to lambda_2 x_2 and its normalization omits x_0.
The prose says transition T4 fell from 30 to 20 time units, while Table 11 gives T4 the delay 10 and T3 the delay 30.
The incidence matrix has a stray 1 in row 3, column 6.
